Cardiac Catheterization SeminarPart 1 · The anatomy you need first

The heart, its chambers and its crown

Learning objectives
By the end of this presentation, students will be able to:
  1. Describe the basic structure of the heart, including its chambers, valves, and layers.
  2. Explain the pathway of blood flow through the heart and the role of coronary arteries in supplying the heart muscle.
Today's route · bars show how much each topic matters for catheterization
Topic 1 · General introductionP5position · size · function

A hollow muscular pump in the middle mediastinum

Function
A hollow muscular organ that pumps blood into the big vessels, with enough force to reach all parts of the body.
Position
Inside the pericardium, in the middle mediastinum, behind the body of the sternum & 2nd–6th costal cartilages.
Side of midline
⅓ : ⅔
⅓ to the right, ⅔ to the left of the median plane.
Size & weight
250–300 g
Slightly larger than a closed fist.
Shape
Conical: a base (posterior surface) and an apex. Its axis runs downwards, forwards and to the left.
Parts
4 chambers: right & left atria, right & left ventricles. 3 surfaces, 4 borders, 1 apex.
Axis of the heart: from base to apex — downwards, forwards and to the left.
Mediastinum: from the root of the neck to the diaphragm, between sternum (front), thoracic vertebrae (back) and the pleurae & lungs (sides).
Borders matter for reading the heart's shadow on X-ray (lines approximate).
Topic 2 · Chambers & valvesP4click a chamber or a valve

Two atria receive, two ventricles pump

Atrioventricular valves
Tricuspid (right) · bicuspid / mitral (left). Cusps tied by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles — 3 in the RV, 2 in the LV.
Semilunar valves
Pulmonary & aortic — at the start of the arteries leaving the heart, 3 cusps each. All valves keep flow one-way.
Topic 3 · Oxygenated & deoxygenated bloodP52 circuits in series

Blue in through the right, red out through the left

1

Pulmonary: right heart → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → gas exchange in lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium.
Systemic: left heart → aorta → systemic arteries → exchange in tissues → veins → right atrium.

Topic 4 · Wall layers & pericardiumP2quick look

Three wall layers inside a protective sac

Bridge to the next topic
The epicardium contains fat and the coronary vessels — that is where we will find the coronary arteries, our next topic.
Topic 5 · Coronary arteriesP5why "coronary" · where they start · 3 terms

Two arteries that encircle the heart like a crown

The heart is supplied by two coronary arteries (right & left). They run in the sulci of the heart, encircling it like a crown — hence the name coronary. The myocardium has its own network of blood vessels.
Origin · from the ascending aorta, just above the aortic valve
Right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus (right coronary cusp, RCC)
Left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus (left coronary cusp, LCC)
Three terms you will hear in anatomy
Circumflex
A vessel that winds or bends around a structure. Example: the left circumflex artery (LCX), a branch of the left coronary artery.
Interposed
Lies between two structures. Example: the RCA passes between the pulmonary trunk and the right auricle.
Anastomosis
A connection between two or more blood vessels. Example: the RCA ends by joining the circumflex artery.
